title: A deep energy method formulation for phase-field modelling of ductile fracture
authors: Nojus Plungė, Peter Brommer, Rachel S. Edwards, Emmanouil G. Kakouris
abstract: This work extends the Deep Energy Method to phase-field modelling of ductile fracture in elasto-plastic solids. Its key contribution is an incremental DEM-based formulation that couples history-dependent J2 plasticity and plasticity-dependent fracture toughness with separate energy-optimised displacement and phase-field representations. The formulation combines the second-order Ambrosio-Tortorelli phase-field fracture model with small-strain J2 plasticity and linear isotropic hardening. A volumetric-deviatoric split defines the elastic crack-driving energy, while accumulated equivalent plastic strain governs the degradation of local fracture toughness. Plastic internal variables are updated locally through radial return. The reduced energy is minimised alternately with respect to the displacement and phase fields, represented by a ReZero residual neural network and spatially localised Gaussian radial basis functions with trainable centres, respectively. This split addresses the diffuse phase-field profiles observed in preliminary calculations with a shared global network. Alternating optimisation is combined with transfer learning to reuse trainable parameters and optimiser states across loading increments, while the converged constitutive history is carried forward separately at quadrature points. The numerical results demonstrate close agreement with finite-element reference solutions in predicting force-displacement responses, energy evolution, plastic deformation and crack propagation. The framework captures the main features of ductile fracture, although accuracy becomes more sensitive to loading increments near abrupt fracture events.

infographic.key_insight: An incremental Deep Energy Method can model ductile fracture by coupling J2 plasticity and phase-field damage with separate neural representations for displacement and crack phase-field.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a mesh-light alternative for predicting fracture initiation and growth in elasto-plastic solids while retaining key constitutive history effects.
method: Alternates energy minimization for displacement and phase-field variables at each load increment.
Uses a ReZero residual network for displacement and localized Gaussian radial basis functions for the phase field.
Updates plastic history locally with radial return and carries constitutive state forward via transfer learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method matches finite-element reference results closely for force-displacement response, energy evolution, plastic deformation, and crack propagation.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy becomes more sensitive to the size of loading increments near abrupt fracture events, so stable increment control is important.
infographic.paper_title: A deep energy method formulation for phase-field modelling of ductile fracture

title: Orientation-Resolved Nanoindentation of Single Crystal Ti-15Mo: Inverted Elastic Anisotropy and Yield-Onset Behavior Beyond Simple CRSS Predictions
authors: Kidus Abebe, David Gaetano, Aurelia Moriyama-Gurish, Jana Šmilauerová, Yanfei Gao, Udo D. Schwarz
abstract: Ti-15Mo (wt%) is a well-established $β$-stabilized alloy whose mechanical response is strongly governed by phase stability and deformation mechanisms that operate at the single-grain scale. Because these intragranular mechanisms are intrinsically anisotropic, understanding the orientation dependence of the elastic and plastic response is critical to the texture-engineered processing of wrought components. Here, we quantify the nanomechanical anisotropy of single-crystal Ti-15Mo by combining EBSD with nanoindentation to correlate hardness, indentation modulus, strain rate sensitivity, and indentation yield response with the crystallographic surface normal near $\langle111\rangle,\langle124\rangle,\langle011\rangle,\langle023\rangle$, and $\langle013\rangle$ directions. While the modulus anisotropy is small (~10%), contrary to the prediction for a cubic crystal with A>1, orientations near $\langle111\rangle$ exhibit the lowest moduli. Yield onset is likewise softest near $\langle111\rangle$ and spans 41%, while hardness spans only 6.6% and follows neither the modulus nor the yield ordering. The alloy also exhibits yield behavior not captured by the simple CRSS/Schmid-factor models evaluated here. Strain-rate-jump tests yield V*=18-31b$^3$, consistent with kink-pair-nucleation-controlled plasticity; based on V*, the orientations separate into two groups suggestive of glide-dominated versus twin/transformation-participating response. We reveal an inversion of the elastic anisotropy expected for a homogeneous cubic $β$-phase and an orientation-dependent yield-onset response that is not reproduced by the simple Schmid-factor models examined here. Retained athermal $ω$ is proposed as the contributor because $β\rightarrowω$ collapse occurs on {111}$_β$ planes and may provide anelastic compliance through the reversible $ω\rightarrowβ$ transformation.

infographic.key_insight: Single-crystal Ti-15Mo shows weak but inverted elastic anisotropy and strongly orientation-dependent yield onset that simple Schmid/CRSS rules do not predict.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For β-titanium component design and texture engineering, crystal orientation can shift indentation modulus and yield behavior enough to matter even when hardness changes only slightly.
method: EBSD to index surface normals and select orientations near ⟨111⟩, ⟨124⟩, ⟨011⟩, ⟨023⟩, and ⟨013⟩
Nanoindentation to measure hardness, indentation modulus, yield onset, and strain-rate sensitivity
Strain-rate-jump testing to estimate activation volume and infer deformation mechanisms
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the sampled orientations, modulus varied by about 10%, yield onset by 41%, and hardness by only 6.6%, with activation volumes of 18–31 b³.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed retained athermal ω-phase explanation is plausible but indirect, so confirming the mechanism would require dedicated phase/structural evidence beyond indentation data.
infographic.paper_title: Orientation-Resolved Nanoindentation of Single Crystal Ti-15Mo: Inverted Elastic Anisotropy and Yield-Onset Behavior Beyond Simple CRSS Predictions

title: A physics-coupled graph neural operator for mid-plane six-component stress tensor field prediction in concrete penetration
authors: Wenpu Du, Peng Zhou, Yunlong Xia, Sinuo Xin, Congcong Zhang, Boyang Zhang
abstract: The penetration-resistant design of concrete structures requires the spatiotemporal evolution of the stress field within the target, whereas in design only the strength grade, the geometry and the projectile parameters are known, and the aggregate arrangement is not. Empirical formulae and scalar-output surrogates serve design screening, and mesoscale finite element models resolve the aggregate-scale response, but one solution cannot cover random aggregate samples at scale, and no framework links mesoscale heterogeneity to field-level prediction. A physics-coupled graph neural operator (PC-GNO) is proposed, which learns in function space the evolution of the mid-plane six-component stress tensor field. The training data are generated by full-scale, aggregate-resolved finite element models and comprise 359 cases at the impact velocities of 100, 135 and 165 m/s, corresponding to compressive strengths of 14, 23 and 48 MPa; the data source is verified by laboratory measurements. The coupling strength of message passing is constructed from the impedance contrast across the material interface, and the update is constrained by spectral normalization. Under the single-step primary setting, the mean accuracy of the three levels is 80.16% (91.45%, 77.80% and 71.22%), i.e. 27.81, 42.46 and 34.16 percentage points above the preceding-frame field of the same window; with 20 664 parameters it exceeds the 87.9% of the best Fourier neural operator configuration (about 812 times as many parameters) and the 71.0% of the closed-form linear regression. The output is the complete six-component tensor field rather than a fixed engineering quantity, so that strength criteria and energy indicators follow from one set of weights. For field-level response prediction in concrete penetration, this result provides a data-driven route, with conditions of applicability defined by the training and the evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: PC-GNO learns the full mid-plane six-component stress tensor field in concrete penetration by coupling graph message passing with physics-informed interface strength.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables surrogate field prediction for penetration-resistant concrete design, letting engineers derive multiple failure and energy metrics from one model instead of relying on scalar outputs or expensive mesoscale FEM runs.
method: Aggregate-resolved finite element simulations generate training fields for 359 impact cases.
Graph message passing is weighted by impedance contrast across material interfaces.
Spectral normalization constrains updates for stable operator learning in function space.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model is trained and evaluated on verified laboratory-backed data at 100, 135, and 165 m/s across concrete strengths of 14, 23, and 48 MPa, achieving 80.16% mean accuracy and outperforming the prior-frame baseline, Fourier neural operator, and linear regression.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is tied to the specific training/evaluation regimes and aggregate-resolution assumptions, so transfer to different concretes, projectile types, or geometries may require retraining or revalidation.
infographic.paper_title: A physics-coupled graph neural operator for mid-plane six-component stress tensor field prediction in concrete penetration

title: LizTail: Unifying Shape Adaptation and Spatial Parallelism with Segment-Reconfigurable Systolic Arrays
authors: Gang Liu, Chen Yang, Junyan Hu, Jianguo Chen, Lixin Duan
abstract: Systolic arrays are widely used to accelerate neural-network inference, yet fixed two-dimensional arrays struggle with the substantial diversity in both matrix geometry and available parallelism across CNNs and Transformer-based large language models. This mismatch is particularly severe for skinny matrices, small-batch autoregressive decoding, and operators containing multiple independent partitions, leading to low processing-element (PE) utilization and repeated spatial folding. Existing reconfigurable arrays typically improve either shape adaptation or distributed execution, whereas supporting both through fine-grained routing incurs considerable interconnect, buffering, and control overheads. We present LizTail (named after lizard tail autotomy, where predefined fracture planes allow segments to detach and remain independently active, analogous to LizTail's predefined reconfiguration boundaries), a multi-mode systolic array that enables constrained segment-level reconfiguration by partitioning a $128\times128$ array into 32 regular $128\times4$ segments and adding connectivity only at predefined endpoints. The resulting substrate supports trimming, long-path extension through $180^\circ$ turn-back connections, and distributed execution in which each subarray can itself be trimmed or extended. Differentiated PE datapaths and segment-aware CEB/SIB buffers provide the required compute and data-delivery flexibility without unrestricted PE-level routing. A hardware-constrained mapper selects the execution organization, dataflow, task partition, and tiling. Across representative workloads, LizTail achieves geometric-mean speedups of $5.02\times$ on CNN inference and $25.67\times$ on LLM decoding over a TPU-like array, while reducing EDP by up to $38.23\times$. LizTail is open-sourced at https://github.com/kmjbwxa/LizTail.

infographic.key_insight: LizTail shows that a systolic array can be made both shape-adaptive and parallelism-aware by reconfiguring computation in predefined segments instead of at individual PEs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for CNNs and LLM decoding because it improves utilization on skinny matrices, small-batch workloads, and multi-partition operators without the full overhead of fully flexible interconnects.
method: Partitions a 128×128 array into 32 fixed 128×4 segments.
Adds only endpoint connectivity, including trimming, 180° turn-back extension, and distributed execution across segments.
Uses differentiated PE datapaths plus segment-aware CEB/SIB buffers, guided by a hardware-constrained mapper.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports geometric-mean speedups of 5.02× on CNN inference and 25.67× on LLM decoding over a TPU-like array, with EDP reduced by up to 38.23×.
infographic.watch_item: The design depends on constrained segment-level reconfiguration, so performance may be limited by mapper quality and by the overheads of implementing segment-aware buffers and endpoint connections in hardware.
infographic.paper_title: LizTail: Unifying Shape Adaptation and Spatial Parallelism with Segment-Reconfigurable Systolic Arrays

title: Low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations
authors: Joy Saha, Jun Yang, Peimeng Yin
abstract: In this work, we develop low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations and incorporate them into a basis-update \& Galerkin mass-lumped finite element method (\mbox{BUG-MLFEM}). By incorporating mass lumping via Gauss-Lobatto quadrature, the spatial discretization yields a matrix differential equation equipped with diagonal positive-definite mass matrices. We establish the weighted dynamical low-rank approximation (WDLRA) within the Galerkin framework of the MLFEM system, proving the theoretical equivalence between the BUG integrator and MLFEM on low-rank subspaces, which guarantees the discrete well-posedness of the implicit BUG steps. To overcome the severe computational bottleneck of standard $O(m^3+n^3)$ Sylvester solvers, we develop tailored, low-cost non-iterative solvers that exploit the inherent sparse-by-small algebraic structure. Under Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions (BCs), the large coefficient matrices are banded, enabling efficient diagonalization of the small $r \times r$ factor matrix and reducing the per-step computational complexity to $O((m+n)r^2)$ and storage to $O((m+n)r)$. For periodic BCs, we combine this diagonalization strategy with a rank-2 Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update to handle wrap-around corner entries at negligible additional cost. Numerical experiments demonstrate first-order temporal and $(k+1)$th-order spatial convergence of the proposed BUG-MLFEM in the discrete $L^2$ norm, where $k$ denotes the polynomial degree of the finite element space, together with significant computational speedups over existing low-rank integrators.

infographic.key_insight: The paper combines weighted dynamical low-rank approximation with a mass-lumped finite element BUG integrator and introduces non-iterative Sylvester solvers to make reaction-diffusion simulation much cheaper without losing the low-rank structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables faster, lower-memory time integration of PDE-based models, making reduced-order simulation more practical for large reaction-diffusion problems under common boundary conditions.
method: Use mass-lumped FEM with Gauss-Lobatto quadrature to obtain diagonal positive-definite mass matrices.
Formulate weighted dynamical low-rank approximation inside the Galerkin framework and prove equivalence with BUG on low-rank subspaces.
Replace costly iterative Sylvester solves with tailored non-iterative solvers, plus a rank-2 Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update for periodic boundaries.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports first-order temporal convergence and $(k+1)$th-order spatial convergence in discrete $L^2$, along with significant speedups over existing low-rank integrators.
infographic.watch_item: The efficiency gains rely on structured sparse/banded operators and careful treatment of boundary conditions, so performance may be less direct for less-structured geometries or discretizations.
infographic.paper_title: Low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations

title: Neural Spline Flow Diffeomorphisms for Pullback Finite Element Methods on Complex Domains
authors: Ioannis Kalogeris, Anaksagoras Spitas, Konstantinos Atzarakis, George Stavroulakis, Vissarion Papadopoulos
abstract: We propose a method for solving partial differential equations on complex domains by learning smooth, invertible mappings from a fixed reference domain using Neural Spline Flows (NSFs). Monotone rational-quadratic spline coupling layers ensure a strictly positive Jacobian determinant by construction, eliminating the need for Jacobian-sign penalties. A diffeomorphic pullback transfers the weak form of the PDE to the reference domain, enabling finite element analysis on reusable structured meshes. To generalize across shapes, a shared NSF is conditioned on low-dimensional latent codes learned through an auto-decoder framework; a subsequent encoder predicts these codes for unseen geometries in a single forward pass. For a given learned map, the pullback preserves the mathematical structure of the PDE and is exactly equivalent to solving on the domain represented by that map. Because the learned domain generally approximates the target geometry, geometric mapping error remains distinct from finite element discretization and quadrature errors. Numerical benchmarks show that sufficiently accurate learned mappings yield reliable finite element solutions. By avoiding repeated generation of unstructured meshes, the method addresses a bottleneck in simulation workflows. The fixed reference mesh also creates opportunities for efficient assembly, memory-aligned data access, and precomputed quadrature. The resulting framework assigns geometric complexity to the neural network while retaining conventional finite element discretization and convergence properties on the learned domain, with overall accuracy also governed by geometric fidelity.

infographic.key_insight: A neural spline flow learns a smooth, invertible map from a fixed reference mesh to complex geometries so finite element PDEs can be solved on a reusable structured domain.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This removes much of the repeated meshing burden in simulation workflows while preserving standard FEM discretization on the learned pullback domain.
method: Use monotone rational-quadratic spline coupling layers to guarantee a positive Jacobian and diffeomorphic mapping.
Transfer the PDE weak form to a reference domain and solve it with conventional finite elements on a structured mesh.
Condition a shared flow on latent shape codes, with an encoder predicting codes for unseen geometries in one pass.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks in the abstract indicate that when the learned geometry is sufficiently accurate, the pullback FEM produces reliable solutions.
infographic.watch_item: Overall accuracy depends on geometric fidelity, so mapping error can remain a separate source of solution error even if the FEM discretization is well resolved.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Spline Flow Diffeomorphisms for Pullback Finite Element Methods on Complex Domains

title: LLM2R: From Large Language Models to 3D Reassemblers
authors: Zhouhan Zhong, Qiuhong Shen, Xingyi Yang, Jinyi Xu, Xinchao Wang
abstract: 3D part assembly aims to reconstruct a complete shape from a set of unassembled parts by predicting a rigid SE(3) transformation for each part. Because the placement of a part is rarely determined by its own geometry, the task demands reasoning over the entire part set, and existing methods, which rely on pairwise relations or iterative generation and verification, scale poorly to objects with many parts. We present LLM2R, which casts part assembly as sequence modeling with a pretrained decoder-only large language model (LLM): a Point-BERT encoder and a Q-Former compress each part into a block of geometric tokens, the blocks of all parts are concatenated, and a causal LLM adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) processes the sequence in one forward pass. Causal attention, however, lets the hidden states of a part observe only the parts that precede it. LLM2R therefore appends a block of learnable summary tokens after the last part: these tokens follow every part, so their states aggregate the whole assembly at a constant token cost, and a part-aware pose head fuses each part's states with them before predicting its rotation and translation. One architecture thus handles semantic and geometric assembly and predicts all poses in a single non-autoregressive pass. LLM2R achieves the highest part accuracy and success rate on all three PartNet categories, the best rotation error, translation error, and part accuracy on PartNeXt, and the lowest translation error and fastest inference on Breaking Bad, where only a fracture-specialized method is more accurate. Its advantage grows with the number of parts: at 100 parts it exceeds GARF by 33.5 points in part accuracy on Breaking Bad and Assembler by 29.1 points on PartNet, and it transfers zero-shot to unseen categories with more than 16 points higher part accuracy than the strongest of three baselines.

infographic.key_insight: LLM2R reframes 3D part assembly as a single-pass sequence modeling problem with a pretrained decoder-only LLM, using summary tokens to collect global context for all parts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a scalable way to reconstruct fractured or disassembled shapes with many parts, improving pose prediction speed and robustness for CAD, robotics, and damage-reassembly workflows.
method: Encode each part with Point-BERT + Q-Former into geometric token blocks
Concatenate all part tokens and process them with a LoRA-adapted causal LLM in one forward pass
Append learnable summary tokens so every part can access global assembly context before pose prediction
infographic.evidence_signal: The method reports top performance on three PartNet categories, PartNeXt, and Breaking Bad, with especially large gains as part count increases and faster inference on Breaking Bad.
infographic.watch_item: Because causal attention is directional, earlier part states cannot directly use later-part context except through the appended summary tokens, so performance may depend on token ordering and summary-token design.
infographic.paper_title: LLM2R: From Large Language Models to 3D Reassemblers

title: FEM-Validated Real-Time Modelling of Soft Tactile Deformation
authors: Silvia Terrile, Kaichen Shi, Taejun Kwon, Jiseok Lee, Nathan Lepora, Yeejin Lee
abstract: Accurate modelling of soft tactile sensors remains difficult because finite element methods (FEM) are computa- tionally expensive, while real-time simulators often lack fidelity for hyperelastic deformation. Large physical datasets are also impractical to collect because repeated testing can damage fragile sensors. We present a data-efficient framework that combines limited real-world validation, high-fidelity FEM, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for accurate real-time prediction of two-dimensional tactile deformation in a planar soft tactile structure. The key idea is to decouple validation from training: 82 camera-tracked contact configurations are used only to tune and validate an ANSYS FEM model, which then generates 768 synthetic contact scenarios for GNN training. We evaluate both forward prediction from marker deformation to contact localisation and inverse inference from contact configuration to marker deformation. The validated FEM achieves sub-0.5 mm error in more than 90% of validation cases, while the learned GNN surrogate reaches a mean absolute error of 0.32 mm with millisecond-scale inference, compared with minute-scale FEM simulation. Models trained entirely on synthetic FEM data retain sub-millimetre accuracy on real measurements from the 2D tactile structure, demonstrating strong sim-to-real transfer within the tested planar setting. We further integrate the learned model into a real-time visualisation pipeline, enabling rapid deformation prediction for virtual prototyping and simulator-based design exploration without extensive physical testing.

infographic.key_insight: A small set of real measurements can be used to validate a high-fidelity FEM model, then generate synthetic data to train a fast GNN surrogate for soft tactile deformation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables millisecond-scale tactile deformation prediction for design exploration and real-time visualisation without needing large physical datasets or repeated sensor testing.
method: Use 82 camera-tracked contact cases to tune and validate an ANSYS FEM model.
Generate 768 synthetic contact scenarios from the validated FEM.
Train GNN surrogates for forward and inverse tactile deformation prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The validated FEM achieved sub-0.5 mm error in over 90% of validation cases, and the GNN reached 0.32 mm mean absolute error with millisecond inference.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstrated sim-to-real performance is limited to the tested planar 2D tactile structure, so broader geometries or loading conditions may need retraining or new validation.
infographic.paper_title: FEM-Validated Real-Time Modelling of Soft Tactile Deformation

title: Deep Learning-based Mechanical Characterization of Synthetically Generated Plant Fibers under Transverse Compression
authors: Nikolaos Kegkeroglou, Bilal Sabillah, Myrto Inglezou, Vincent Placet, Céndric Clevy, Antonios Porichis
abstract: Plant fibers are increasingly used as sustainable reinforcements in composites, but the intrinsic variability of their microstructure causes substantial scatter in transverse mechanical behavior, complicating composite design. Characterizing this behavior relies on finite element (FE) simulations requiring several minutes of high-performance computing per fiber, making high-throughput characterization across realistic fiber populations impractical. In this study, we propose a deep learning framework replacing this FE bottleneck with a fast pipeline. It includes two coupled recursive U-Nets predicting the step-by-step evolution of fiber deformation and internal stress fields under transverse compression, followed by a regression CNN estimating the transverse Young's modulus from the final stress field. Unlike prior approaches predicting stress fields for fixed configurations or idealized geometries, our framework recursively resolves the full temporal stress evolution for synthetic fibers derived from real hemp cross-sections, with or without a lumen. Trained on 1,000 synthetic fiber geometries with FE ground truth, it reproduces the stress field sequence with a Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) of $0.9574 \pm 0.0074$ and a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of $0.0345 \pm 0.0079$. It estimates transverse Young's modulus with an $R^2$ of $0.938 \pm 0.024$, a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of $24.31 \pm 1.23$ MPa, and a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of $5.25 \pm 0.91\%$. Inference requires under one second per fiber versus five minutes per FE simulation, drastically reducing computational cost. This offers a fast, reliable tool for mechanical characterization of synthetic plant fibers, with promising applications in designing natural fiber-reinforced composites.

infographic.key_insight: A recursive deep-learning pipeline can replace slow finite-element simulations to rapidly predict how plant fibers deform and carry stress under transverse compression.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables high-throughput mechanical screening of realistic natural-fiber geometries, supporting faster design of sustainable composite materials.
method: Two coupled recursive U-Nets predict step-by-step deformation and internal stress evolution.
A regression CNN estimates transverse Young's modulus from the final stress field.
The model is trained on 1,000 synthetic hemp-fiber geometries with FE ground truth.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the abstract-reported test results, the stress-field sequence was reproduced with SSIM 0.9574 ± 0.0074 and RMSE 0.0345 ± 0.0079, while modulus prediction achieved R² = 0.938 ± 0.024, MAE = 24.31 ± 1.23 MPa, and MAPE = 5.25 ± 0.91%.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated on synthetic fiber geometries derived from hemp cross-sections, so robustness to unseen species, manufacturing defects, and broader loading conditions still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Learning-based Mechanical Characterization of Synthetically Generated Plant Fibers under Transverse Compression

title: An algebraic multiscale framework for two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners
authors: Filipe Cumaru, Hadi Hajibeygi, Cornelis Vuik, Alexander Heinlein
abstract: The robustness of two-level overlapping additive Schwarz (OAS) preconditioners for highly heterogeneous elliptic problems hinges on the choice of the coarse space. We propose an algebraic multiscale (AM) coarse space built from the system matrix alone through an algebraic formulation of the multiscale finite element method (MsFEM). The coarse basis functions are energy-minimizing extensions of the solutions of reduced boundary condition (RBC) problems on the subdomain interface, so that coefficient variations along the interface enter the coarse space. By posing the RBC problems on slabs that extend the interface, the construction also applies to general unstructured domain decompositions. Embedding the AM formulation in an energy-minimizing framework extends it to linear elasticity, and we show that existing condition number bounds for OAS with MsFEM coarse spaces carry over to the algebraic setting. For problems with high coefficient inclusions on the coarse nodes, the AM iteration count and condition number are unaffected by increasing the contrast. In 3D scalar diffusion with log-normal coefficients, AM needs about as many iterations as the generalized Dryja--Smith--Widlund (GDSW) coarse space, while solving a coarse problem ten times smaller. For linear elasticity, omitting the coarse basis functions associated with the rotational rigid body modes yields a fully algebraic coarse space that still scales well for homogeneous problems.

infographic.key_insight: The paper builds a fully algebraic multiscale coarse space for two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners by using reduced boundary-condition interface problems and energy-minimizing extensions, making the coarse correction robust to strong heterogeneity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a matrix-based preconditioner that can improve scalability for heterogeneous diffusion and elasticity problems without requiring explicit multiscale finite-element mesh construction.
method: Construct the coarse space from the system matrix alone via an algebraic MsFEM formulation.
Solve reduced boundary condition problems on interface slabs, then extend them by energy minimization.
Embed the framework in an energy-minimizing form so it also applies to linear elasticity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that, for high-contrast inclusions on coarse nodes, iteration counts and condition numbers stay unchanged as contrast increases, and in 3D log-normal diffusion the method matches GDSW iteration counts with a coarse problem about 10× smaller.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on how well the interface-based slabs and coarse-node selection capture rigid-body and heterogeneity effects, especially for elasticity and unstructured decompositions.
infographic.paper_title: An algebraic multiscale framework for two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners

title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 2D
authors: Tommaso Bevilacqua, Axel Klawonn, Martin Lanser, Adam Wasiak
abstract: Two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners with Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW) and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces for high-order finite element methods (FEM) and virtual element methods (VEM) are investigated and applied to the Poisson problem in 2D. The GDSW coarse space is a well-established robust choice for preconditioners in domain decomposition, while the RGDSW coarse space offers a competitive alternative by reducing the coarse problem dimension while maintaining robustness. On the theoretical side, a condition number bound for both preconditioners is proved for conforming $\mathbb{P}_k$ and $\mathbb{Q}_k$ finite element spaces with explicit dependence on the polynomial degree $k$. Through numerical experiments on structured triangular and quadrilateral meshes for FEM and on polygonal meshes for VEM, it is demonstrated that both GDSW and RGDSW maintain scalability properties across polynomial orders up to $k=9$ for selected degrees. The RGDSW approach achieves a reduction in the coarse problem dimension by a factor of approximately three compared to GDSW while maintaining competitive iteration counts.

infographic.key_insight: Two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW and RGDSW coarse spaces remain robust for high-order 2D Poisson discretizations, while RGDSW significantly shrinks the coarse problem size.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a scalable preconditioning strategy for high-order FEM/VEM solvers, helping keep iteration counts stable as polynomial order increases.
method: Build two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with overlap.
Use GDSW or reduced GDSW coarse spaces for P_k, Q_k FEM and VEM.
Derive condition-number bounds with explicit dependence on polynomial degree k.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests on structured triangular/quadrilateral FEM meshes and polygonal VEM meshes show scalable performance up to k=9, with RGDSW cutting coarse dimension by about 3x while keeping competitive iterations.
infographic.watch_item: The reported robustness is shown for the 2D Poisson model problem, so performance on more complex PDEs or 3D geometries still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 2D

title: Refurbishment and Cryocooler Upgrade of the CPAPIR Wide-Field Near-Infrared Camera: Design, Integration, and Lessons Learned
authors: Philippe Vallee, Jonathan St-Antoine, Lison Malo, Frederique Baron, Sylvie F Beaulieu, Rene Doyon
abstract: The CAmera PAnoramique Proche Infrarouge (CPAPIR) is a wide-field near-infrared imager that has been operating at the Observatoire du Mont-Mégantic (OMM) since 2004. After more than two decades of service, the instrument required a major refurbishment due to detector degradation, including the loss of one quadrant, as well as operational constraints associated with its liquid-nitrogen cooling system. To extend the instrument's lifetime and reduce maintenance requirements, the detector was replaced and the cooling system upgraded through the integration of a Sunpower CryoTel DS30 cryocooler. This paper presents the thermal and mechanical redesign of the instrument, including finite element analysis (FEA), three-dimensional CAD modeling, hardware selection, and laboratory validation. Particular attention is given to the challenges encountered during integration and testing, notably vibration mitigation and cryogenic system implementation. The resulting performance improvements and lessons learned from the upgrade are discussed. The upgraded instrument is scheduled for on-sky commissioning at the Observatoire du Mont-Mégantic in summer 2026.

infographic.key_insight: CPAPIR was refurbished by replacing a degraded detector and converting its cooling from liquid nitrogen to a cryocooler-based system to extend instrument life and improve operability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The upgrade shows how thermal-mechanical redesign, FEA, and hardware integration can modernize aging scientific instruments while reducing maintenance burden.
method: 3D CAD redesign of the detector and cryocooler integration
Finite element analysis to assess thermal and mechanical performance
Laboratory validation with attention to vibration mitigation and cryogenic implementation
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports successful design, integration, and lab testing of the upgraded system, with on-sky commissioning planned for summer 2026.
infographic.watch_item: Cryocooler integration can introduce vibration and alignment challenges that must be managed carefully during commissioning.
infographic.paper_title: Refurbishment and Cryocooler Upgrade of the CPAPIR Wide-Field Near-Infrared Camera: Design, Integration, and Lessons Learned

title: Stable-Plastic Subspace Construction for Differentially Private Continual LoRA
authors: Jin Liu, Ning Xi, Yinbin Miao, Junkang Liu, Ke Cheng, Jianfeng Ma
abstract: Continual learning (CL) adapts pretrained models to a sequence of tasks while retaining knowledge acquired from earlier tasks. When task data are sensitive, differential privacy (DP) provides record-level protection, but maintaining both adaptation and retention under privacy constraints remains challenging. We study this problem in continual low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and observe that: 1) private training increases forgetting primarily during subsequent adaptation rather than initial task acquisition; 2) jointly perturbing both LoRA factors introduces a non-negligible bilinear noise interaction; and 3) DP aggravates the stability-plasticity dilemma, hindering both knowledge retention and adaptation to new tasks. Based on these observations, we propose DP-SPA, which constructs a stable subspace from previously privatized updates and a plastic subspace from pretrained weights within its orthogonal complement. The method fixes these bases and privately optimizes only the LoRA factor, eliminating the bilinear noise interaction within each step. Before merging each task update, it rescales stable-direction coefficients using historical and current update energies. We establish a privacy guarantee and show that recalibration does not increase historical overlap and tightens a conditional upper bound on old-task loss increase. Experiments across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets show that DP-SPA improves average accuracy and reduces forgetting compared with the evaluated baselines.

infographic.key_insight: DP-SPA preserves continual LoRA performance under differential privacy by separating learned updates into a stable subspace for retention and a plastic subspace for new-task adaptation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For privacy-sensitive engineering models, this offers a practical way to update pretrained systems across tasks while reducing forgetting and avoiding privacy-induced degradation in adaptation.
method: Build a stable subspace from previously privatized updates.
Define a plastic subspace in the orthogonal complement of pretrained weights.
Privately optimize only one LoRA factor per step and recalibrate stable coefficients using historical/current update energy before merging.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets, with improved average accuracy and reduced forgetting over baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on correctly estimating and maintaining the stable/plastic subspace structure, which may add implementation complexity and sensitivity to subspace quality.
infographic.paper_title: Stable-Plastic Subspace Construction for Differentially Private Continual LoRA

title: Continual Learning for Reliable In-Sequence Molecular Communication
authors: Siddhant Setia, Junichi Suzuki, Tadashi Nakano
abstract: This paper considers reliable in-sequence molecular communication, where bio-nanomachines exchange molecule-encoded information in a specified order, and investigates a new simulation-based method to incrementally evaluate communication protocols by gradually increasing the complexity of experimental settings. The proposed method, called Affine Memory Replay (AMR), builds a continual learning (CL) model to estimate communication performance between bio-nanomachines. AMR stores past simulation samples and synthesizes additional replay samples through interpolation and extrapolation between past samples. Through incremental performance estimation tasks, it replays both past and synthetic samples to regularize model updates, helping the model adapt to new experimental settings while retaining knowledge from earlier ones. Experimental results show that AMR significantly outperforms existing CL methods in maintaining overall estimation accuracy across sequentially learned estimation tasks. It effectively balances memory stability and learning plasticity under moderate training cost.

infographic.key_insight: Affine Memory Replay (AMR) uses continual learning with replayed and synthesized past simulations to keep molecular communication performance estimates accurate as experimental settings become more complex.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables reliable, incremental evaluation of bio-nanomachine communication protocols without retraining from scratch, supporting scalable design and testing of molecular communication systems.
method: Stores past simulation samples in memory
Generates replay samples by interpolation and extrapolation between past samples
Replays real and synthetic samples during sequential training to preserve earlier knowledge while learning new settings
infographic.evidence_signal: In incremental performance estimation tasks, AMR outperformed existing continual learning methods in overall accuracy while maintaining a balance between stability and plasticity under moderate training cost.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on the quality and representativeness of stored samples and synthetic interpolation/extrapolation, which may be sensitive in highly non-linear or out-of-distribution settings.
infographic.paper_title: Continual Learning for Reliable In-Sequence Molecular Communication

title: Generalization of Strang-Fix remark for discrete maximum principles on tetrahedral meshes
authors: Safdar Ali, Maksat Ashyraliyev, Sergey Korotov, Sergei Silvestrov
abstract: Most of qualitative properties of finite element (FE) approximations for various PDE models, in particular the validity of the discrete maximum principles (DMPs), are usually guaranteed by certain geometric properties (e.g. acuteness/nonobtuseness) of FE meshes used. In this work, we revisit the linear FE discretization of the Poisson equation and discuss, in the context of DMPs, the representation of the stiffness matrix entries in terms of the edge lengths and cotangents of the dihedral angles of the tetrahedral meshes, thus avoiding the common use of face areas and element volumes. Using this type of entry representation, certain structural properties of meshes, and simple trigonometric relations, as proposed in the two-dimensional case by Strang and Fix, we show that DMPs still hold (as the stiffness matrices remain $M$-matrices) for many tetrahedral configurations with obtuse dihedral angles. Such a relaxation of the standard acuteness/nonobtuseness conditions can be vital in practical calculations, as these angle properties are difficult to preserve in global and local mesh refinements. Several representative examples are presented.

infographic.key_insight: By expressing tetrahedral FE stiffness entries through edge lengths and dihedral cotangents, the paper extends Strang-Fix-style reasoning to prove discrete maximum principles for many meshes even when some dihedral angles are obtuse.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This relaxes strict mesh-acuteness requirements for Poisson simulations, making DMP-preserving finite element meshes easier to use in practical 3D engineering workflows.
method: Recast stiffness-matrix entries using edge lengths and cotangents of tetrahedral dihedral angles.
Apply structural mesh relations and simple trigonometric identities in the Strang-Fix spirit.
Show that the resulting stiffness matrices remain M-matrices for a broad class of tetrahedral configurations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports representative examples demonstrating that the relaxed geometric conditions still preserve discrete maximum principles.
infographic.watch_item: The result is still mesh-geometry dependent, so identifying or generating admissible tetrahedral meshes in complex 3D domains may remain challenging.
infographic.paper_title: Generalization of Strang-Fix remark for discrete maximum principles on tetrahedral meshes

title: DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Dynamics on GPU
authors: Kemeng Huang, Bowen Ren, Xinyu Lu, Minchen Li, Taku komura
abstract: Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable enforcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or positional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration through geometric barriers and {continuous collision detection (CCD)}. However, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid components retain many vertex {degrees of freedom (DoFs)}. We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interacting deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable {rest-shape} design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients account for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Experiments demonstrate peak speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0x with full-space FEM and 4133.3x with affine bodies for combined forward simulation and backward differentiation.

infographic.key_insight: DiffGIPC makes contact-aware inverse mechanics much faster by combining IPC’s non-penetration guarantees with GPU-accelerated differentiation and a low-DoF affine-body formulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables practical optimization of deformable and nearly rigid systems for design, identification, placement, and articulated control without sacrificing contact fidelity.
method: Uses Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) with geometric barriers and continuous collision detection to enforce non-penetration.
Introduces affine-body derivatives so nearly rigid bodies use only 12 motion DoFs while still supporting rest-shape, initial-state, and control optimization.
Computes a coupled FEM-affine adjoint per frame and accelerates backward passes on GPU through a PyTorch interface.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports peak end-to-end speedups of about 150.0x over DiffIPC for full-space FEM and 4133.3x with affine bodies for forward simulation plus backward differentiation.
infographic.watch_item: The workflow still depends on accurate CCD/contact handling and GPU-efficient implementation, so robustness and performance may vary with complex contact scenes or parameter mappings.
infographic.paper_title: DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Dynamics on GPU

title: Nanoscale Mapping of Strain-engineered Excitons in Monolayer WSe$_2$
authors: Anna S. Roche, Nicholas V. Proscia, Paul D. Cunningham, Kathleen M. McCreary, Dante J. O'Hara, Hsun Jen Chuang
abstract: Excitons in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are highly sensitive to external stimuli, allowing control of resonance energies and lifetimes through electric and magnetic fields, heterostructures, moire potentials and mechanical strain. Observations of single-photon emission (SPE) near sample edges, wrinkles, and strained nanobubbles have motivated strain-engineering aimed at realizing localized emitters in 2D materials. The origin of these emitters remains unclear and prior studies have relied on far-field spectroscopy with strain profiles inferred separately through topography, limiting direct correlation between local strain and excitonic response. We directly probe strain-modified excitonic spectra in monolayer WSe$_2$ using cryogenic scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM). We compare two strain-engineering techniques, nano-indentation and patterned substrates, used to produce SPEs. At 9 K, we spatially resolve exciton resonance shifts with sub-diffraction limit resolution, simultaneously measuring near-field optical response and topography. We observe that strain transferred from nano-indentation into a deformable polymer substrate differs from that produced by draping TMDs over patterned dielectric pillars. Adhesion and tearing during plastic deformation drive a compressive exciton blueshift, while draping produces dominant tensile strain. Comparing the strain model results to the experimentally observed energy shifts shows that the nano-indentation strain is over an order of magnitude smaller than previously inferred, due to puncturing of the fragile monolayer, whereas pillar-strained devices remain intact under more modest strain. These differences suggest SPE arises from complex, strain-mediated interactions rather than simple confinement potentials, establishing s-SNOM as a powerful probe of quantum emission in strained 2D materials.

infographic.key_insight: Cryogenic s-SNOM can directly map how nanoscale strain alters exciton energies in monolayer WSe2, revealing that different strain-engineering routes produce very different local responses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For strain-engineered 2D optoelectronic devices, the work shows that achieving reliable single-photon emitters depends on controlling not just strain magnitude but also damage, adhesion, and deformation mode.
method: Compared nano-indentation and patterned-substrate strain engineering in monolayer WSe2.
Used 9 K scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy to measure near-field optical response and topography simultaneously.
Correlated local exciton resonance shifts with strain model predictions at sub-diffraction resolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The measured exciton energy shifts showed that nano-indentation produced strain more than an order of magnitude smaller than previously inferred, while pillar-based devices remained intact under more modest tensile strain.
infographic.watch_item: Interpretation depends on accurately separating true strain effects from puncturing, tearing, and adhesion-driven deformation in fragile monolayers.
infographic.paper_title: Nanoscale Mapping of Strain-engineered Excitons in Monolayer WSe$_2$

title: Specialized machine learning force fields for materials dynamics
authors: Yue Wu, Haoyu Wan, Yuan Tian, Deng Pan, Mingwei Chen
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are transforming atomistic simulations by accessing unprecedented length and time scales. While pretrained equivariant graph neural networks achieve robust zero-shot performance for near-equilibrium properties across broad chemical spaces, their translation to complex materials dynamics remains fundamentally challenged by out-of-distribution reactive states, representation biases, and computational scaling limits. In this Review, we examine how physics-driven specialization extends the applicability of MLIPs to complex dynamical systems. We systematically evaluate the structural trade-offs in MLIP design: the undersampling of highly strained configurations, the prohibitive computational overhead of high-order message-passing architectures, and the necessity of nonlocal interactions for open and field-coupled systems. Through four demanding application contexts - electrified interfaces, compositionally fluctuating open systems, multiphase evolution, and large-scale fracture - we establish a framework for observable-specific validation. Highlighting the complementary roles of universal foundation models and task-specific potentials, we emphasize that targeted adaptations must be rigorously benchmarked against intended observables. We conclude with a roadmap for developing physically consistent, hardware-aware force fields that seamlessly connect electronic-structure accuracy to macroscopic materials phenomena.

infographic.key_insight: Specialized ML force fields extend machine-learning interatomic potentials beyond near-equilibrium prediction by adding physics-driven adaptations for reactive, nonlocal, and highly strained materials dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For fracture and damage modeling, the paper argues that force fields must be chosen and validated against the specific observable of interest, not just general benchmark accuracy.
method: Assess MLIP design trade-offs: strained-state coverage, message-passing cost, and nonlocal interaction handling.
Map performance to four demanding settings: electrified interfaces, open systems, multiphase evolution, and large-scale fracture.
Compare universal foundation models with task-specific potentials using observable-specific benchmarks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The review synthesizes and evaluates evidence across four challenging application contexts to test whether specialized potentials remain accurate for the intended dynamical observables.
infographic.watch_item: Specialized models can fail outside their training distribution, and high-order or nonlocal architectures may introduce major computational overhead and hardware constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Specialized machine learning force fields for materials dynamics

title: SPARS: A Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection Framework for Continual Learning
authors: Teif Aldaajani, Huda Hakami, Maha A. Thafar
abstract: Continual learning aims to acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned knowledge. However, updating shared parameters when learning new tasks often overwrites existing knowledge, causing catastrophic forgetting. Memory replay methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting but rely on previous samples, raising privacy, memory, and scalability concerns. On the other hand, parameter isolation-based methods preserve learned knowledge but may limit knowledge transfer, whereas regularization promotes adaptability but remains susceptible to interference between old and new tasks. To maintain the stability-plasticity trade-off, this paper proposes Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection (SPARS), a replay-free hybrid framework combining global parameter isolation with localized parameter regularization. SPARS estimates parameter importance using either the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) or a novel Confidence Score (CS) estimator that leverages logit sensitivity and achieves comparable performance to FIM without requiring labelled data. Based on parameter importance, SPARS partitions parameters into three importance-aware regions namely, winning, neighboring, and non-important parameter regions. Each region receives a different adaptation strategy: selective freezing, soft regularization, or unrestricted learning based on its role in the stability-plasticity trade-off. To mitigate classifier bias in class-incremental learning, we employ Quadratic Discriminant Analysis to improve performance on previously learned classes .Experiments on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet demonstrate consistent improvement in average incremental accuracy over existing isolation- and regularization-based methods across task- and class-incremental learning. On TinyImageNet, SPARS achieves the best performance with 6% improvement for class-incremental learning while retaining over 60% of parameters for future tasks.

infographic.key_insight: SPARS improves continual learning by splitting parameters into importance-aware regions and applying different stability-plasticity controls to each region.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a replay-free way to reduce catastrophic forgetting while preserving adaptability, which is useful for scalable learning systems in engineering applications.
method: Estimate parameter importance using FIM or a label-free Confidence Score based on logit sensitivity.
Partition parameters into winning, neighboring, and non-important regions.
Apply selective freezing, soft regularization, or unrestricted updating per region; use QDA to reduce class bias.
infographic.evidence_signal: On CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet, SPARS consistently improved average incremental accuracy over isolation- and regularization-based baselines, with a reported 6% gain on TinyImageNet class-incremental learning.
infographic.watch_item: Region assignment and importance estimation may add tuning complexity, and performance could depend on how well the thresholds transfer across datasets and task settings.
infographic.paper_title: SPARS: A Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection Framework for Continual Learning

title: Discrete Edge Multiscale Space based Hybrid Schwarz Preconditioner for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
authors: Shubin Fu, Shihua Gong, Guanglian Li, Yueqi Wang
abstract: In this work, we develop a novel hybrid Schwarz method, termed as edge multiscale space based hybrid Schwarz (EMs-HS), for solving the Helmholtz problem with large wavenumbers. The problem is discretized using $H^1$-conforming nodal finite element methods on meshes of size $h$ decreasing faster than $k^{-3/2}$ such that the discretization error can be bounded by the data uniformly with respect to $k$. EMs-HS consists of a one-level Schwarz preconditioner (RAS-imp) and a coarse solver in a multiplicative way. The RAS-imp preconditioner solves local problems on overlapping subdomains with impedance boundary conditions in parallel, and combines the local solutions using partition of unity. On the PDE level, this coarse space corresponds to an edge multiscale space proposed in {[S. Fu, G. Li, R. Craster, and S. Guenneau, \emph{Multiscale Model. Simul.}, 19(4):1684-1709, 2021]}. The approximation properties of this coarse space to the discrete solutions from the primal and adjoint problems are derived by a novel conforming Galerkin finite element method based upon a nonstandard variational formulation. This work represents the first theoretical analysis of an edge multiscale space at the discrete level. We prove that the EMs-HS preconditioner leads to a convergent fixed-point iteration uniformly for large wavenumbers, by rigorously analyzing the approximation properties of the coarse space to the global Helmholtz harmonic extension part and to the solution of the adjoint problem. We provide extensive numerical results on the sharpness of the theoretical findings and also demonstrate the method on challenging heterogeneous models.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces an edge-multiscale coarse space inside a hybrid Schwarz preconditioner that remains effective for high-frequency Helmholtz problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a scalable solver strategy for wave simulations where standard domain decomposition methods struggle as the wavenumber grows.
method: Use overlapping subdomains with impedance-boundary local solves (RAS-imp) in parallel.
Add a coarse correction built from an edge multiscale space derived at the discrete level.
Prove uniform convergence by analyzing approximation of primal, adjoint, and harmonic extension components.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive numerical experiments that test the sharpness of the theory and demonstrate performance on challenging heterogeneous models.
infographic.watch_item: The method relies on sufficiently fine meshes for the Helmholtz discretization, with h decreasing faster than k^{-3/2}, which may raise cost for very large wavenumbers.
infographic.paper_title: Discrete Edge Multiscale Space based Hybrid Schwarz Preconditioner for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
